content_voiceover: This diagram maps the three pathophysiologic drivers of thalassemia complications, which is a favorite board framework for predicting end-organ damage from first principles. Everything starts with the impaired alpha to beta globin ratio, which branches into ineffective erythropoiesis, hemolysis, and, in transfused patients, iron loading from transfusion itself. Ineffective erythropoiesis and hemolysis both increase iron and free radicals, and hemolysis also directly causes anemia and gallstones from chronic bilirubin turnover. The anemia then drops tissue oxygenation, raising EPO and driving erythroid marrow expansion, which explains the extramedullary hematopoietic pseudotumors, hepatosplenomegaly, and bone deformities with osteoporosis that you see on exam and imaging. Meanwhile the iron overload pathway, amplified by increased gut iron absorption from ineffective erythropoiesis, deposits in endocrine organs and drives diabetes, growth deficiency, hypothyroidism, hypoparathyroidism, and hypogonadism, plus the newer additions of hepatic cancer and renal disease. Separately, hemolysis and marrow expansion together create a hypercoagulable state, explaining the increased risk of leg ulcers, thrombotic events, and pulmonary hypertension leading to right heart failure. The exam takeaway: if you know the three arms, iron overload, marrow expansion, and hypercoagulability, you can predict virtually every thalassemia complication without memorizing a list.
keypoints: 3 core mechanisms: ineffective erythropoiesis, hemolysis, iron overload
Iron overload → endocrinopathies (DM, hypothyroid, hypogonadism), cirrhosis
Marrow expansion → hepatosplenomegaly, bone deformity, pseudotumors
Hemolysis + marrow expansion → hypercoagulable state → thrombosis, PHTN
keypoint_voiceover: The exam framework has three arms stemming from the impaired globin ratio: iron overload drives endocrinopathies and liver disease, erythroid marrow expansion drives hepatosplenomegaly and bone deformities, and the hypercoagulable state from hemolysis plus marrow expansion drives thrombosis, leg ulcers, and pulmonary hypertension. Knowing these three arms lets you predict any thalassemia complication logically instead of memorizing a list.
